summary_paragraph: A young woman with a history of congenital tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, tracheostomy, and chronic respiratory colonization with MRSA and Pseudomonas was admitted for worsening cough, neck pain, odynophagia, and green tracheal discharge. Initial evaluation revealed tenderness and swelling at the trach site, but imaging showed only mild laryngeal edema without abscess, and labs showed no leukocytosis. Sputum and bronchial cultures grew MRSA and Pseudomonas, but minimal inflammatory cells suggested colonization rather than active infection. Antibiotics were discontinued after infectious disease consultation. Pain was managed with IV morphine initially, then transitioned to oral oxycodone and tramadol. The trach tube was replaced by interventional pulmonology, and ENT confirmed no tracheitis. Supportive care included hypertonic saline nebulizers, bronchodilators, and saline drops via trach. She was discharged home with instructions to use a heat-moisture exchanger during the day, humidified air at night, and scheduled saline drops, along with follow-up with pulmonary and ENT specialists.
